summary: This unit gives you the calculations a Level 3 welder and fabricator uses every day: units and conversions, formulas and how to rearrange them, percentages, ratios, rates and costs, Pythagoras and trigonometry for frames, stairs and braces, areas and paint, volumes, capacities and masses, weld metal, consumables, heat input and machine speeds, and tolerances, scales and simple statistics. You will also learn to set out and check your working so that a mistake is caught before steel is cut.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 3 you work out the numbers for a job yourself: the cut lengths and angles of a frame, the mass of a load before it is lifted, the weld metal and gas to order, the paint for a tank, the heat input on a procedure, and whether a batch of parts is within tolerance.

A wrong number in fabrication is expensive and sometimes dangerous: a brace cut 100 mm short, a load heavier than the crane, a disc spun faster than it is rated for. This unit teaches the methods and, just as important, the habits that catch mistakes: units on every number, a rough estimate, and a second person's check.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You need a scientific calculator (with π, square root, sin, cos and tan keys, set to degrees).

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the shop
rows: Work in metric units, convert between mm, m, mm², m², cm³, m³ and litres, and convert imperial figures from imported drawings and procedures.
Put numbers into a formula in the right order, and rearrange it to find any quantity, such as travel speed from heat input.
Work with percentages, ratios and rates
Work out waste, discounts, mark-ups, errors, reject rates, gas mixtures, cutting times and gas use.
Use Pythagoras and sin, cos and tan for braces, stringers, ramps and rafters, and check frames for square.
Plates with holes, gussets, curved rails, tank surfaces, paint, tank capacities and the mass of plate, bar and pipe.
Fillet throats and areas, weld metal volume and mass, electrodes and wire to order, heat input, gas, arc time and disc rim speeds.
Decide whether parts are within tolerance, read scale drawings, and work out the mean, median, mode and range.
Write the working step by step with units, round sensibly, check by estimate and by working back, and have it checked.

ul: A **multiple-choice paper**: mostly short calculations (formulas, percentages, triangles, areas, masses, weld metal, tolerances, statistics, conversions), plus questions on why answers are checked.

A **written paper**: short answers that need an exact number with its unit, or a term (hypotenuse, mean); and longer worked problems where you must show each step, such as rearranging the heat input formula or finding a brace length and angle.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: measure a fabricated item and calculate its mass, weld metal, paint and materials cost, then weigh it and compare; and set out, cut and check a braced frame using Pythagoras and trigonometry.

blocks.note: In the written paper, most marks are for the working. Write the formula, then the numbers in it, then the answer with its unit. A correct method with a slip in the arithmetic still earns most of the marks; a bare wrong answer earns none.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Quantity
Units in the shop
Key facts
rows: mm on drawings; m for stock and site
mm² for sections and welds; m² for plate and paint
mm³ and cm³ for weld metal; m³ and litres for tanks and steel
Steel about 7 850 kg/m³ = 7.85 g/cm³ = 7.85 kg per litre
Flowmeters in the shop read L/min
mm/min for travel and cutting; m/s for disc rims

blocks.note: For areas and volumes, the length conversion is squared or cubed. Because 1 m = 1 000 mm, 1 m² = 1 000² mm² = 1 000 000 mm², and 1 m³ = 1 000³ mm³ = 1 000 000 000 mm³. Most big slips in mass and paint sums come from this.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Conversion
Example
rows: 35 ft³ an hour = 35 × 28.3 = 990.5 L an hour; ÷ 60 = about 16.5 L/min

blocks.note: Much of the steel, machinery and paperwork in Jamaican shops comes from the USA, so you will meet inches, pounds, psi, °F and cubic feet per hour. Write the unit beside every figure, convert carefully, and get approval before replacing an imperial plate or pipe size with the 'nearest' metric one: it may be thinner.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Work in the order **BODMAS**: Brackets first, then Orders (powers and roots), then Division and Multiplication from left to right, then Addition and Subtraction from left to right. On a calculator, put brackets round the top and the bottom of a fraction: (24 × 150 × 60) ÷ (1 000 × 120), not 24 × 150 × 60 ÷ 1 000 × 120. Set the calculator to degrees (D or DEG) before any sin, cos or tan.

ul: Write down the full calculator result, and round only at the end.
Round to a sensible accuracy: cut lengths to the nearest 1 mm (a tape reads 1 mm), mass to 0.1 kg, plate and paint areas to 0.01 m².
Round **up** for things you buy or use whole: lengths of stock, sheets, tins, cylinders. 2.1 sheets means 3 sheets.
Example: a calculator shows 1 247.63 mm for a brace; write 1 248 mm on the cut list.

**Rough estimate:** round the numbers and work it in your head. A plate 2.5 m × 1.25 m × 6 mm is about 3 m² × 0.006 m = 0.018 m³, and × 8 000 kg/m³ is about 144 kg. The exact answer, 147.2 kg, agrees; 1 472 kg or 14.7 kg would show a slip.
**Work backwards:** put the answer back into the formula and see whether you get the starting figure.
**Sense check:** a brace must be longer than either side of its triangle but shorter than the two added together; a preheat of 900 °C is not sensible.
**Second method:** a scale drawing, a table, or a different formula.
**Another person:** for anything that matters, a team member checks and initials the working.

flow: Heading: what is being worked out, for which job, drawing and part
Data: each figure with its unit and where it came from (drawing, table, maker's data)
Change all figures to the same units
The same formula with the numbers in it
Answer with its unit, rounded sensibly
Check: estimate, work back or sense check
Sign and date; checker initials; file with the job

blocks.p: A **formula** is a rule written with letters. To use it, put each number in place of its letter (**substitution**), with the units the formula expects, then work it out in BODMAS order.
To make a different letter the subject, **do the same thing to both sides** until that letter is on its own:

ul: Something **multiplies** the letter: divide both sides by it.
Something **divides** the letter, or the letter is on the bottom: multiply both sides by it.
Something is **added**: subtract it from both sides. Something is **subtracted**: add it to both sides.

head: Formula
Make this the subject
Result
rows: Plate mass m = L × W × t × ρ

blocks.p: Many welding procedures limit the heat put into a weld, because too much heat can weaken some steels and too little can cause cracking or poor fusion. A common formula is:
**HI (kJ/mm) = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1 000 × S)**, where V is the arc voltage in volts, I the current in amps and S the travel speed in mm/min.

head: Example
Working
Answer
rows: Travel speed needed to keep at or below 1.0 kJ/mm at 26 V and 190 A
296 mm/min: travel at least this fast

blocks.p: Heat input goes up in step with the volts and the amps, and down as the travel speed goes up. Double the speed and the heat input halves; raise the current by 10% and the heat input rises by 10%.

blocks.note: Some codes and procedures multiply arc energy by a thermal efficiency factor for the process. Use exactly the formula and units your WPS or the code the Centre uses gives, and show which one you used.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Direct:** twice the length of weld needs twice the weld metal; twice the arc time uses twice the gas.
**Inverse:** twice the cutting speed halves the cutting time; twice the number of welders (doing the same kind of work) roughly halves the days.

head: Type
Method
Example
rows: 12% waste on 85 m: 85 × 12 ÷ 100 = 10.2 m, so order 95.2 m
One amount as a percentage of another
Gas from J$5 200 to J$5 720: 520 ÷ 5 200 × 100 = 10% increase
A price of J$46 000 after a 20% increase was 46 000 ÷ 1.2 = about J$38 333 before

blocks.p: **Mark-up** is profit as a percentage of the **cost**. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the **selling price**. They are not the same.

blocks.h: A materials price, step by step

blocks.p: GCT is added at the **current rate** to the final price of the whole job and shown on its own line. To add a percentage, multiply by (1 + the rate ÷ 100).

ul: A ratio compares parts. A shielding gas of 80% argon and 20% carbon dioxide is 80 : 20, which simplifies to **4 : 1**. A 3 : 1 mix is 3 ÷ 4 = 75% and 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.
Paint thinned 5 : 1: in 6 litres of mix there are 5 litres of paint and 1 litre of thinner.
To share an amount in a ratio, add the parts, divide, then multiply: J$36 000 shared 2 : 1 is J$24 000 and J$12 000.

head: Rate
Formula
Example
rows: 10 500 L at 15 L/min = 700 min, about 11.7 h of arc time
2 h 40 min (2.67 h) of arc in an 8 h shift: about 33%

blocks.note: Turn hours and minutes into decimal hours before multiplying: 2 h 40 min is 2 + 40 ÷ 60 = 2.67 h, not 2.4 h.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Braces, stair stringers, ramps, rafters and gussets all make right-angled triangles. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is the **hypotenuse**.
**c² = a² + b²**, so c = √(a² + b²), and a short side a = √(c² − b²).

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Brace across a frame 1 800 × 900 mm (centre lines)
Level going of a stringer 3 400 mm long that rises 1 800 mm

ul: A triangle with sides in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 has a right angle. Mark 600 mm along one side and 800 mm along the other: if the diagonal between the marks is 1 000 mm, the corner is square. 900, 1 200 and 1 500 mm works too.
A rectangular frame is square when its two **diagonals are equal**. If one is longer, push the ends of the longer diagonal towards each other until both read the same.
For a frame w × h, each diagonal should be √(w² + h²).

blocks.p: The **opposite** side faces the angle θ; the **adjacent** side runs beside it (not the hypotenuse). To find an angle from a ratio, use the inverse key: θ = tan⁻¹(opposite ÷ adjacent), and the same with sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹.

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Ramp rising 450 mm at 6°: length along the slope
Brace rising 750 mm over 1 300 mm: angle to the level
about 30°; the other end angle is 90° − 30° = 60°
Rafter 4.2 m long at 18°: rise and run

ul: Slope as a percentage = rise ÷ level run × 100. A rise of 150 mm over 2 000 mm is 7.5%.

Slope as a ratio: '1 in 12' means 1 unit of rise for every 12 of level run, which is 8.3%, or an angle of tan⁻¹(1 ÷ 12) = about 4.8°. A percentage and an angle are different things: an 8.3% slope is not 8.3°.

head: Step
Working
Answer
rows: Frame 1 200 × 900 mm outside, in 40 × 40 mm square tube; posts run full height, rails fit between them
2 posts at 900 mm; 2 rails at 1 120 mm
Brace from inside corner to inside corner
Brace angle to the bottom rail
Check diagonals of the outside of the frame

blocks.note: A brace length worked out between centre lines is not its cut length. Decide which lines the brace really fits between (centre lines, inside faces), allow for the member sizes and the end cuts, mark the end angles from the triangle, and offer the brace up before cutting a batch.

head: Shape
Area
Perimeter or length
rows: π × d × (angle ÷ 360); a quarter circle is π × d ÷ 4
π × (D² − d²) ÷ 4, outside D, inside d
curved side π × d × h; each flat end π × r²

blocks.p: Use π = 3.142 unless the question gives another value. Radius r is half the diameter d.

Working
Answer
rows: Plate 1 500 × 1 000 mm with two 150 mm holes
Gusset, a right-angled triangle with 250 mm sides at the right angle
Handrail bent in a half circle of radius 600 mm
Outside of an open-top tank, 1.6 m diameter, 1.2 m high: side and bottom

blocks.p: **Litres of paint = area × number of coats ÷ coverage per litre per coat.**

ul: Example: 8.04 m², 2 coats, 9 m² per litre: 8.04 × 2 ÷ 9 = 1.79 litres.
Round **up** to the tin sizes sold, and allow for losses: rough or pitted steel, spraying and wind take more than the tin says.
Use the coverage printed by the paint maker; it differs between primers and topcoats.
Inside and outside means twice the area; two coats doubles it again.
For tube and sections, the outside area is the perimeter × the length: a 50 × 50 mm square tube has about 0.2 m² of outside surface per metre.

blocks.note: Paint in Jamaica is often sold by the US gallon (about 3.8 litres) and the quart (about 0.95 litre) as well as in litres. Check the size on the tin before you work out how many to buy. Paint for the inside of a drinking-water tank must be a type made for drinking water.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Mass = volume × density.** Use m³ with kg/m³, or cm³ with g/cm³: never mix them.
Densities: steel about 7 850 kg/m³; stainless steel about 7 900–8 000 kg/m³; aluminium about 2 700 kg/m³; water 1 000 kg/m³.
**Capacity:** 1 m³ holds 1 000 litres, and 1 litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg.
The inside diameter of a pipe = outside diameter − 2 × wall thickness.

head: Job
Working
Answer
rows: Round bar 32 mm diameter, 3 m long
Pipe 88.9 mm outside, 5.5 mm wall: mass per metre
1 980 litres; about 1.98 t of water when full
18 m of tube listed at 4.25 kg/m in the supplier's table

ul: Work out the total mass: the load, plus slings, shackles and any spreader beam.
Compare it with the safe working load (SWL) of the crane or hoist **at the radius used**, and with each sling's rating. Never exceed it, and leave a margin.
Example: 8 plates, each 2.4 × 1.2 m × 10 mm: each is 0.0288 m³ × 7 850 = 226 kg, so 8 weigh about 1 809 kg. On a 2 t hoist that leaves under 200 kg for slings and errors: lift in two batches.

blocks.note: A full water tank is far heavier than the steel that holds it up: a 2 000-litre tank holds about 2 tonnes of water. Stands and towers are designed for the full load, and a calculated mass is checked by estimate before anything is lifted.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: For a flat-faced fillet weld with equal legs z, the cross-section is a right-angled triangle. The **throat** a is about **0.7 × z** (more exactly 0.707), and the **area is ½ × z²**.
Real welds are usually a little convex or oversize, so add an allowance (often 10–20%) when estimating weld metal.

For a single-V butt weld, the area is the gap times the thickness, plus the V. With a 60° included angle, the V is (t − root face)² × tan 30°. Example: 10 mm plate, 2 mm gap, 1.5 mm root face: 2 × 10 = 20 mm², plus (8.5)² × 0.577 = 41.7 mm², total about 62 mm², plus the cap and root reinforcement.

flow: Area of the weld cross-section (mm²), with an allowance for oversize
× total weld length in mm = volume in mm³
÷ the deposition efficiency = mass of electrodes or wire to draw
Round up to whole packets or spools

blocks.p: Example: 15 m of 8 mm fillet. Area 32 mm² + 15% = 36.8 mm². Volume 36.8 × 15 000 = 552 000 mm³ = 552 cm³. Mass 552 × 7.85 = 4 333 g, about 4.3 kg.

head: Process
Typical share of the consumable that ends up as weld metal
rows: Often about 55–65%: stub ends, spatter and the flux coating are lost. For 4.3 kg of weld: 4.3 ÷ 0.6 = about 7.2 kg of electrodes

blocks.note: These efficiency figures are typical only: use the maker's data and your shop's own records, and follow your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Gas, arc time and duty cycle

ul: Gas used = flow (L/min) × arc time (min). Shielding gas only flows while the arc burns (plus pre-flow and post-flow), so use arc time, not shift time.
Cylinder life = contents ÷ flow. Do not plan to empty a cylinder completely: keep a spare ready.
Duty cycle: 35% at 200 A means 3.5 minutes of welding in every 10 at that current.

blocks.p: **Rim speed (m/s) = π × d (in metres) × rev/min ÷ 60.** A 125 mm disc on a grinder running at 11 000 rev/min: 3.142 × 0.125 × 11 000 ÷ 60 = about 72 m/s.

blocks.note: Every cutting and grinding disc is marked with its maximum speed in m/s and rev/min. Never fit a disc whose rated speed is lower than the grinder's no-load speed: it can burst. Use the disc size the grinder and its guard are made for.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A size of **450 ± 1.5 mm** may be anything from 448.5 to 451.5 mm. These are the **limits**; the difference between them (3 mm) is the **tolerance band**.
A one-sided tolerance such as **Ø25 +0.3 / −0** means 25.0 to 25.3 mm: never smaller than 25.0.
A part exactly on a limit passes; anything beyond it fails.
On a 1 : 20 drawing, 1 mm on paper is 20 mm on the job. Real size = drawing size × 20; drawing size = real size ÷ 20.
Example at 1 : 25: a line 46 mm long on paper is 46 × 25 = 1 150 mm on the job. At 1 : 20, a real 2 400 mm is drawn 2 400 ÷ 20 = 120 mm long.
Use the written dimensions wherever they are given. Paper stretches and copies shrink, so do not measure ('scale') off a drawing for cutting unless there is no other way, and then check.

head: Measure
How to find it
Example: 601, 599, 600, 603, 598, 600, 602 mm
rows: Add them up and divide by how many there are
Put them in order and take the middle one
The value that appears most often

blocks.p: The mean shows whether a batch is centred on size; the range shows how much it spreads. If the range is wider than the tolerance band, some parts must be outside the limits, even when the mean is right on size. Look for the cause: a loose saw stop, a worn tape, or different people measuring in different ways.

Percentage difference = (measured − calculated) ÷ calculated × 100. For example, a frame calculated at 148 kg weighs 152 kg: 4 ÷ 148 × 100 = about 2.7% heavier. Likely reasons: weld metal and paint left out of the sum, steel slightly thicker than its nominal size, and rounding.

ul: Put the measurements in a table, with the limits, and mark each part pass or fail.
Give the mean, the range and the number (and percentage) outside tolerance.
Set aside and label the failed parts, check the rest of the batch, and say what you think the cause is.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say 'I can' to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can convert between mm, m, mm², m², mm³, cm³, m³ and litres, and between imperial and metric units.
I can use a calculator in the right order of working, with brackets and in degrees.
I can round sensibly, and round up when buying stock, sheets, tins or cylinders.
I can check an answer by estimate, by working back and by sense, and set out my working for another person to check.
I can substitute into a formula and rearrange it, including the heat input formula.
I can work out percentages of amounts, percentage change and error, discounts, waste and reject rates.
I can tell mark-up from margin, and build a materials price with waste, mark-up and GCT at the current rate.
I can use ratios for gas mixtures and mixing, and rates for cutting time, gas use and cylinder life.
I can use Pythagoras and the 3-4-5 rule, and check a frame by its diagonals.
I can use sin, cos and tan to find sides and angles of braces, ramps, stringers and rafters.
I can find areas of plates, gussets, rings and cylinders, and the paint needed.
I can find volumes, capacities and masses of plate, bar, pipe and tanks, and check a load against a safe working load.
I can work out fillet throats and areas, weld metal mass and the electrodes or wire to order.
I can work out disc rim speed and check a disc's rating.
I can use tolerances and scales, and find the mean, median, mode and range of a batch.

terms: Adjacent side
In a right-angled triangle, the side next to the angle being used (not the hypotenuse)
Density
Mass per unit volume; steel is about 7 850 kg/m³
Deposition efficiency
The share of an electrode's or wire's mass that ends up as weld metal
Heat input
The heat put into a weld per millimetre of length, worked out from volts, amps and travel speed
Hypotenuse
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle
Leg length
The size of a fillet weld measured from the root to the toe
Limits
The largest and smallest acceptable sizes
Margin
Profit as a percentage of the selling price
Mark-up
Profit as a percentage of the cost
Mean
The average: the total divided by the number of values
Median
The middle value when the values are put in order
Mode
The value that appears most often
Opposite side
In a right-angled triangle, the side facing the angle being used
Pythagoras' rule
In a right-angled triangle, c² = a² + b²
Range
The largest value minus the smallest
Rim speed
The speed of the edge of a turning disc, in m/s
Safe working load (SWL)
The most a crane, hoist or sling may lift
Scale
The ratio between the size on a drawing and the real size
Throat
The depth of a fillet weld from the root to the face; about 0.7 × the leg
Tolerance
The amount a size may vary from the size on the drawing
Transposition
Rearranging a formula to make another quantity the subject

c1.title: A water tank for a clinic in Christiana
c1.text: A shop is making a closed cylindrical steel water tank for a clinic in Christiana, Manchester. It is 1.4 m in inside diameter and 1.6 m high, and the shell, top and bottom are about 10.1 m² of 4 mm plate. The empty tank will be lifted onto its tower with a hoist rated at 500 kg SWL, using slings that weigh 15 kg. Use π = 3.142 and steel at 7 850 kg/m³.

c2.title: A stair and a ramp in Bull Bay
c2.text: At a community centre in Bull Bay, St Andrew, a team is making a steel stair, a wheelchair ramp and a landing frame. The stair stringers climb 1 650 mm over a level going of 2 200 mm. The ramp must rise 300 mm at a slope of 1 in 12. The rectangular landing frame is 2 400 mm by 1 800 mm, and it is to be checked for square before it is welded.

c3.title: A bracket order in Yallahs
c3.text: A shop in Yallahs, St Thomas, is making 120 brackets. Each bracket has 250 mm of 6 mm fillet weld with equal legs, made with MIG. The welder's records show a gas flow of 15 L/min and about 1.5 minutes of arc time per bracket. Weld metal is 7.85 g/cm³.

c4.title: An imported procedure at a pipe shop near Rockfort
c4.text: At a pipe shop near Rockfort, Kingston, Jermaine is checking an imported welding procedure. It limits heat input to 1.5 kJ/mm, using HI = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1 000 × S), and asks for a preheat of 175 °F. His test run was made at 24 V and 150 A, travelling at 120 mm/min. Later he must fit a disc to a 230 mm grinder marked 6 600 rev/min.

c5.title: Gate posts in Highgate
c5.text: A shop in Highgate, St Mary, is cutting gate posts to 1 850 ± 2 mm. Tanisha measures eight of them: 1 849, 1 851, 1 853, 1 850, 1 848, 1 850, 1 847 and 1 852 mm. The shop's drawing of the gate is at a scale of 1 : 25.

questions.q: What is the capacity of the tank?
questions.why: Volume = π × r² × h = 3.142 × 0.7² × 1.6 = 2.463 m³, and 1 m³ = 1 000 litres. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives 9 853; forgetting to square the radius gives 3 519.

questions.q: What is the mass of the 4 mm plate in the tank?
questions.why: Volume = 10.1 m² × 0.004 m = 0.0404 m³, and 0.0404 × 7 850 = about 317 kg. The thickness must be in metres (4 mm = 0.004 m) to match the m² and kg/m³.

questions.q: Can the hoist lift the empty tank onto the tower?
o: No: the full tank weighs over 2.7 tonnes, far above 500 kg
Yes: about 332 kg with the slings, which is within 500 kg
No: the plate alone weighs over 3 tonnes, so it is too heavy
Yes: the hoist could lift the tank even when it is full
questions.why: Empty, the tank is about 317 kg; with 15 kg of slings the lift is about 332 kg, under the 500 kg SWL. The water (about 2.46 t) only matters once the tank is on the tower, where the tower must carry it.

questions.q: Each stringer is the sloping side of a right-angled triangle. What is its true length?
questions.why: The stringer is the hypotenuse: √(1 650² + 2 200²) = √(2 722 500 + 4 840 000) = √7 562 500 = 2 750 mm. Adding the two sides (3 850) ignores the right angle; subtracting the squares (1 455) finds a short side.

questions.q: At what angle to the level does the 1 in 12 ramp rise? (tan 4.8° ≈ 0.084, tan 5.7° ≈ 0.100)
questions.why: A 1 in 12 slope has tan θ = 1 ÷ 12 = 0.083, so θ is about 4.8°. 8.3 is the slope as a percentage, not an angle in degrees.

questions.q: If the landing frame is square, what should each of its diagonals measure?
questions.why: Each diagonal is √(2 400² + 1 800²) = √9 000 000 = 3 000 mm, a 3-4-5 triangle. 4 200 mm is the two sides added together.

questions.q: After tacking, the diagonals measure 3 004 mm and 2 996 mm. What should the team do?
o: Nothing: the average of the two is 3 000 mm, so the frame is square
Cut 4 mm off one long side so that the frame matches the drawing
Re-measure with another tape, since diagonals can never differ by 8 mm
Ease the ends of the long diagonal together until both read the same
questions.why: Unequal diagonals mean the frame is out of square, here by 8 mm. Pushing the corners at the ends of the longer diagonal towards each other brings both to 3 000 mm; then weld.

questions.q: What mass of weld metal is in all 120 brackets, before any allowance for oversize?
questions.why: Area ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 mm²; length 120 × 250 = 30 000 mm; volume 540 000 mm³ = 540 cm³; mass 540 × 7.85 = 4 239 g, about 4.2 kg. Using 6 × 6 = 36 mm² for the area doubles the answer.

questions.q: How much shielding gas will the 120 brackets use?
questions.why: Arc time is 120 × 1.5 = 180 minutes, and 180 × 15 L/min = 2 700 litres. Multiplying 120 brackets by 15 L/min (1 800) leaves out the time.

questions.q: The drawing is changed to call for a 5 mm throat. About what leg length gives this?
questions.why: Throat a = 0.7 × leg z, so z = a ÷ 0.7 = 5 ÷ 0.7 = 7.1 mm, about 7 mm. Multiplying by 0.7 (3.5 mm) works the formula the wrong way round.

questions.q: Does Jermaine's test run meet the procedure's heat input limit?
o: Yes: it is about 0.18 kJ/mm, well under the 1.5 limit
No: it is about 1.8 kJ/mm, over the 1.5 kJ/mm limit
Yes: it is about 1.2 kJ/mm, under the limit
No: it is about 18 kJ/mm, far over the limit
questions.why: (24 × 150 × 60) ÷ (1 000 × 120) = 216 000 ÷ 120 000 = 1.8 kJ/mm, which is more than 1.5. Brackets round the top and the bottom stop the calculator slips that give 0.18 or 18.

questions.q: Keeping 24 V and 150 A, what travel speed keeps the heat input within 1.5 kJ/mm?
questions.why: S = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1 000 × HI) = 216 000 ÷ 1 500 = 144 mm/min. Travelling faster puts in less heat, so 144 mm/min is the slowest allowed: at least 144.

questions.q: What is 175 °F in °C?
questions.why: °C = (°F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = (175 − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = 143 × 5 ÷ 9 = 79.4 °C. Forgetting to take away 32 first gives about 97 °C.

questions.q: The grinder's disc rim speed works out at about 79.5 m/s. Which disc may Jermaine fit?
o: A 230 mm disc marked 63 m/s, used with only light pressure
Any 230 mm disc, as long as its centre hole fits the spindle
A 230 mm disc marked 80 m/s and at least 6 600 rev/min
A 125 mm disc, as a smaller disc turns more slowly at its rim
questions.why: A disc's rated speed must be at least the grinder's: 3.142 × 0.23 × 6 600 ÷ 60 is about 79.5 m/s, so an 80 m/s disc is needed. A slower-rated disc can burst, and a small disc does not fit the 230 mm guard and flanges.

questions.q: What are the mean and the range of Tanisha's eight posts?
questions.why: The total is 14 800 mm, and 14 800 ÷ 8 = 1 850 mm. The range is the largest minus the smallest: 1 853 − 1 847 = 6 mm.

questions.q: How many of the eight posts are outside the tolerance?
o: None, because the mean is exactly on size
4 posts, which is 50% of the sample
2 posts, which is 25% of the sample
1 post, which is 12.5% of the sample
questions.why: The limits are 1 848 and 1 852 mm. Posts exactly on a limit pass, so only 1 847 and 1 853 fail: 2 of 8, or 25%.

questions.q: What do the mean and the range together tell Tanisha?
o: The batch passes, since the mean is exactly 1 850 mm
The saw is set long, and its stop should be moved
Only the posts that failed need any further thought
Spread exceeds the 4 mm band; look for the cause
questions.why: The batch is centred (mean 1 850 mm), but its 6 mm range is wider than the 4 mm tolerance band, so parts will keep failing. Look for an unsteady cause: a loose stop, a worn tape or different measuring methods.

questions.q: How long is a 1 850 mm post drawn on the 1 : 25 drawing?
questions.why: Drawing size = real size ÷ 25 = 1 850 ÷ 25 = 74 mm. Multiplying by 25 (46 250) works the scale the wrong way.

questions.q: Steel costs a shop J$40 000 and is sold for J$50 000. Which statement is right?
o: The mark-up and the margin are both 25%
The mark-up is 25% and the margin is 20%
The mark-up is 20% and the margin is 25%
The mark-up and the margin are both 20%
questions.why: The profit is J$10 000. Mark-up is profit ÷ cost = 10 000 ÷ 40 000 = 25%; margin is profit ÷ selling price = 10 000 ÷ 50 000 = 20%.

questions.q: After a 15% discount, an order of steel costs J$51 000. What was the price before the discount?
questions.why: J$51 000 is 85% of the original, so the original is 51 000 ÷ 0.85 = J$60 000. Adding 15% of J$51 000 (J$58 650) uses the wrong base.
